subject: zoology
question_text: How does a mature RBC of a mammal differ from that of other vertebrates?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.56, VSAQ 122). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Mammalian RBC
steps.margin_note: Three shape words in a numbered list. That is the first mark.
lines: A mature red blood cell of a mammal is:
Losing the nucleus leaves more room for
steps.why: Three shape words answer the whole question, and the missing nucleus is the one that explains why a mammal carries more oxygen per cell.
common_mistakes: Writing that the mammalian RBC has a nucleus. The mature cell loses it.
Calling it biconvex. The mammalian RBC is biconcave, which widens the surface.
steps.memory_tip: Round, dented on both faces, and no nucleus: three words for the mammal.

steps.label: RBC of other vertebrates
steps.margin_note: Three opposite words in the same order as the first step. The examiner reads them as a pair.
lines: The mature red blood cell of other vertebrates
steps.why: The other vertebrates take the opposite word at every point, so the pair is learnt as three straight opposites rather than as six separate facts.
common_mistakes: Mixing the two lists. Every word of one list is the opposite of the other.
Writing that birds have no nucleus in the RBC. Birds are nucleated like the rest.
steps.memory_tip: Every word flips: circular to oval, concave to convex, no nucleus to nucleus.

insider_note: Write the two lists in the same order so the three opposites line up; that is what earns full credit in a two mark answer.
